title: Copilot for Meetings — Prep, Notes & Follow-Up

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Meetings consume an enormous share of a knowledge worker's week — and most of that time is wasted on tasks AI can handle: finding background, creating agendas, recording what was said, tracking what was decided, and drafting follow-ups.

Copilot can take over every surrounding task that isn't the actual conversation:
- **Before:** Research attendees, pull relevant context, draft the agenda
- **During:** Structure notes in real time, flag decisions and action items as they're made
- **After:** Extract action items, draft follow-up emails, update task tickets, write decision records

You'll learn:
- Pre-meeting briefing generation
- Agenda creation for different meeting types
- Real-time note structuring
- Action item extraction and tracking
- Automated follow-up email drafting
- Calendar MCP integration

## Before the Meeting: Pre-Meeting Briefing

A pre-meeting briefing gives you context on who you're meeting, what's relevant, and what you need from the meeting before it starts. This is especially valuable for meetings with people outside your immediate team.

### Attendee and Context Research

```
I have a meeting in [X hours] with [attendees and their roles].
The meeting topic is: [topic].

Help me prepare:
1. What are the key things I should understand about [their role/team/project] 
   before this meeting?
2. What questions should I ask to get what I need from this meeting?
3. What do I need to bring or be ready to present?
4. What's the most likely outcome they want from this meeting, and what do I want?
5. What are the 3 most important things to accomplish in the time available?
```

### Pulling Prior Context from Your Systems

With task management MCP connected:
```
Before my meeting about [topic], pull relevant context:
1. Search [ADO/Jira] for any open items related to [topic or project]
2. Find any items assigned to meeting attendees [names] that might come up
3. Are there any blocked items or risks in [project] I should be aware of?
4. What decisions were made last sprint that this meeting might relate to?

Summarise the key things I should know walking into this meeting.
```

### The One-Page Brief

```
Create a one-page meeting brief for me to read 5 minutes before the meeting.

Meeting: [Title]
With: [Attendees and roles]
Duration: [X minutes]
Objective: [What needs to happen in this meeting]
Context: [relevant background]
My goal: [what I specifically want to achieve or decide]

Format:
- Context (3 sentences)
- What I need to know about each attendee's likely position
- 3 most important things to accomplish
- My opening statement (1-2 sentences to set the tone and purpose)
```

## Creating Effective Agendas

A good agenda is more than a list of topics — it's a design for how time will be used, who will speak when, and what decisions will be made.

### Standard Meeting Agenda

```
Create an agenda for a [duration] meeting with [N] people about [topic].

Objective: [what this meeting must accomplish]
Must-cover topics:
- [topic 1]
- [topic 2]
- [topic 3]
Decision needed: [if any — what decision will be made in this meeting]

Format the agenda with:
- Time allocations for each item (must add up to [X] minutes)
- Named facilitator for each item
- Expected output type: Discussion / Decision / Information only
- 5 minutes buffer at end for action items and wrap-up

First item must always be: 'Confirm objective and agenda (2 min)'
Last item must always be: 'Action items and owners (5 min)'
```

### Different Meeting Types

**Decision Meeting:**
```
Create an agenda for a decision meeting.
Decision to make: [specific decision]
Options being considered: [list the options]
Who has a stake in this decision: [attendees and their interest]
What information is needed to decide: [data, analysis, input]

Structure: context → options presentation → discussion → decision → record
No more than 30% of time should be context-setting — the bulk should be on options and discussion.
```

**Retrospective:**
```
Create a team retrospective agenda for a [X minute] session.
Team size: [N people]
Sprint/period covered: [timeframe]
Include: what went well, what didn't, root cause of top problem, 
specific action items for next sprint (not vague 'we should communicate better' items).
Use the 4Ls format: Liked, Learned, Lacked, Longed For.
```

**One-on-One (1:1) with direct report:**
```
Create a 1:1 meeting template for a 30-minute weekly check-in with a direct report.
Areas to cover: their current work and any blockers, their wellbeing, 
my feedback on recent work, their feedback for me, career or development discussion.
Make it a dialogue, not a status report — most of the talking should be them.
```

## During the Meeting: Real-Time Note Structuring

You can't type and participate fully at the same time. But you can type bullet-point fragments and have Copilot structure them into readable notes immediately after — or during a break.

### The Fragment-to-Notes Workflow

**During the meeting, capture raw fragments in a `.md` file:**
```
- J says deadline moving to Jul 15 - budget
- R disagrees - thinks Aug is more realistic
- decision: J to send revised timeline by Thursday
- M raised security review - unresolved
- action: K to schedule security review meeting next week
- next steps: everyone update their items by EOD tomorrow
```

**Immediately after, paste into Copilot:**
```
Structure these meeting notes into a professional format.
Add section headings: Attendees, Key Discussions, Decisions Made, Action Items.
For each action item: [WHO] will [DO WHAT] by [WHEN]
Do not add information I didn't provide — only structure what's there.
Flag any action items where the owner or deadline is missing.
```

### Decision Capture Template

Have this ready to fill during the meeting for any decision made:
```
Decision made: [what was decided]
Date: [today]
By: [who made the decision — named individual, not 'the team']
Options considered: [briefly — what were the alternatives]
Rationale: [why this option]
Implementation: [who will do what by when]
Review date: [when to check if the decision was right]
```

**After the meeting:**
```
I captured this decision during a meeting. Format it as a formal Decision Record 
for our project documentation. Be concise but complete.
[paste the filled template]
```

## After the Meeting: Action Items, Follow-Ups & Tickets

The meeting's value is in what gets done afterward. Copilot can automate every post-meeting task.

### Action Item Extraction

```
Extract all action items from these meeting notes.
Format: | WHO | WHAT | BY WHEN | PRIORITY |
For any action where WHO or WHEN is missing: flag it as [UNASSIGNED] or [NO DEADLINE].
Also identify: any actions that depend on another action completing first.
```

### Creating Tickets from Action Items

```
For each action item in these meeting notes, create a task ticket in [ADO/Jira].
For each ticket:
- Title: action verb + specific deliverable
- Description: context from the meeting about why this is needed
- Assignee: the person identified in the action item
- Due date: the agreed deadline
- Tag: 'meeting-[date]-action-item'

Do not create tickets for items marked as ongoing or standing activities — 
only create tickets for specific, time-bounded actions.
```

### Follow-Up Email to Attendees

```
Draft a follow-up email to meeting attendees summarising:
1. What was decided (bullet points only)
2. Action items — named list with deadlines
3. Next meeting (if scheduled)

Tone: professional, concise. People are busy — don't recap the discussion.
Subject line: [Meeting Name] — Decisions & Actions [DD/MM]
Length: under 200 words. The action item table will add length — keep everything else short.
```

### Follow-Up to Absent Stakeholders

```
Draft a brief update for [name] who couldn't attend the [meeting name] meeting.
They care about: [their specific interest in this topic]
Key things they need to know: [decisions that affect them, actions assigned to them]
Tone: informative, not catching-up — they're busy, give them only what's relevant to them.
```

**Calendar MCP for scheduling.** If your organization uses Google Calendar or Microsoft Outlook Calendar with MCP access, you can ask Copilot to find meeting times: 'Find a 45-minute slot next week when [list of attendees] are all free, preferably morning.' This works well for small groups. For large groups, use your calendar tool's scheduling assistant directly — Copilot works better for context and drafting than for complex availability checking across many calendars.

sections.title: Prepare a Real Upcoming Meeting
sections.content:
Apply the full pre-meeting workflow to a meeting that's actually on your calendar.

**Step 1 — Choose a meeting from this week** that involves preparation or decision-making. Not a routine standup — something with substance.

**Step 2 — Generate the one-page brief:**
```
Create a one-page brief for my upcoming meeting.
Meeting title: [title]
Attendees: [who's coming and their roles]
Duration: [minutes]
My objective: [what I need to achieve]
Background: [any context I can provide]
```

**Step 3 — Draft the agenda:**
```
Create a [duration]-minute agenda for this meeting. 
Objective: [from step 2]
Must-cover items: [list what needs to be discussed]
Decision needed: [yes/no — what decision if yes]
Include time allocations and expected output type for each item.
```

**Step 4 — Pull task context** (if MCP connected):
```
Search [your task system] for any items related to [meeting topic] 
that I should be aware of before this meeting.
```

**Step 5 — Prepare your questions:**
```
Based on the meeting objective and attendees, what are the 5 most important 
questions I should ask during this meeting to achieve the objective?
```

**Step 6 — Attend the meeting.** Take fragment notes during.

**Step 7 — Post-meeting: structure notes and extract actions.**

**Reflect:** Did the preparation change how the meeting went? Were the suggested questions useful? What would you add to your briefing template?

sections.title: Workshop A — Meeting Note Processing
sections.content:
Process a set of real meeting notes from memory or a past meeting.

**Step 1 — Write raw notes.** From memory of a recent meeting, write down fragments in bullet form — exactly like you would have taken during the meeting. Don't structure them — write them as fast as you would have captured them live.

Aim for 15-25 bullets over 2-3 minutes. Include: things discussed, decisions made, who said what, action items (even if incomplete).

**Step 2 — Paste into Copilot and run structure:**
```
Structure these meeting notes. Create sections:
- Attendees mentioned
- Decisions made (numbered list, each with who decided and what was decided)
- Action items (table: WHO | WHAT | BY WHEN)
- Open questions (anything raised but not resolved)
- Context for absent stakeholders (2-sentence summary)

Do not add anything I didn't write down. Flag any action items missing an owner or deadline.
```

**Step 3 — Create the follow-up email:**
```
Draft a follow-up email to meeting attendees from these structured notes.
Include: decisions, action items, and any next meeting date if mentioned.
```

**Step 4 — Create the action item tickets:**
```
From the action items, write 3 ticket descriptions in [ADO/Jira] format.
Each needs: clear title, description with enough context for the assignee, deadline.
```

**Measure:** From raw notes to structured output, email draft, and 3 ticket descriptions — how long did this take? Compare to doing it manually.

sections.title: Workshop B — Build Your Meeting Template Library
sections.content:
Create reusable meeting templates for the 4 most common meeting types in your work.

**Identify your 4 most common meeting types** (examples: weekly team meeting, project review, 1:1, decision meeting, stakeholder briefing, project kickoff).

**For each type, create a template pair:**

**Template 1 — Agenda template** (what you generate before the meeting)
Create `.github/prompts/meeting-[type]-agenda.prompt.md`
Include: standard sections for this meeting type, time allocation guidance, required participants, what to prepare.

**Template 2 — Notes-to-output template** (what you run after the meeting)
Create `.github/prompts/meeting-[type]-notes.prompt.md`
Include: the structure the output should have, what to extract (decisions, actions, risks), the follow-up email format, whether to create tickets.

**For your 1:1 template specifically, add:**
- Tracking section: what was discussed last time, what follow-up was needed
- Development section: any career or growth topics raised
- Sentiment flag: was there anything in the conversation suggesting the person is struggling, disengaged, or frustrated?

**Test each template** with notes from a real past meeting.

**Outcome:** A personal meeting playbook — open the right template, fill in the context, and Copilot handles every surrounding task.

sections.title: Workshop C — Build a Decision Register System
sections.content:
Create a lightweight decision register for your team — a searchable record of every significant decision made, why it was made, and who made it.

**Why this matters in government:** Decisions made in meetings become invisible. When a colleague asks 'why did we do it this way?' or an audit asks for the rationale behind a policy choice, the answer should be findable — not lost in someone's meeting notes from 6 months ago.

**Step 1 — Create `decisions/` folder** in your project repository.

**Step 2 — Create a decision record template**
`.github/prompts/create-decision-record.prompt.md`:
```markdown
Create a decision record from these meeting notes or decision details.

Format: `decisions/YYYY-MM-DD-[short-topic].md`

Content:
# Decision: [one-line title]

**Date:** [YYYY-MM-DD]
**Decision maker:** [named person or named group]
**Project/context:** [project name]

## The Question
[What decision was being made?]

## Options Considered
1. [Option A] — [brief pros/cons]
2. [Option B] — [brief pros/cons]

## Decision Made
[What was decided — one clear statement]

## Rationale
[Why this option over the others — 2-4 sentences]

## Implications
[What changes as a result of this decision]

## Review Trigger
[Under what circumstances should this decision be revisited?]
```

**Step 3 — Process your last 5 significant decisions** through this template. Create a decision record file for each.

**Step 4 — Create a decision index** (`decisions/README.md`) that lists all decisions with one-line summaries.

**Step 5 — Add to team workflow:** After every meeting with a significant decision, Copilot creates a decision record from the meeting notes. Commit it to the repo.

**Outcome:** A searchable, version-controlled decision record — the institutional memory your team currently doesn't have.

sections.question: You take raw meeting notes in fragments during a meeting and immediately ask Copilot to structure them. The output looks good but includes a specific action item assigned to a person who wasn't in the meeting and a deadline that wasn't mentioned. What happened and what should you do?
options: Copilot hallucinated details. Review every structured output against your raw notes before sharing. Remove or flag any information that wasn't in your original fragments.
Your raw notes were unclear — Copilot interpreted them correctly
Copilot accessed your email to find additional context
This is a formatting issue — ask Copilot to re-format the same notes
sections.explanation: AI models can hallucinate — generating plausible but fabricated details, especially when the input is fragmentary or ambiguous. If your raw notes said 'action: K to do X' and Copilot produced 'K to complete X by Friday' but no deadline was mentioned, it invented the deadline. Always compare structured meeting notes against your original fragments before sending to attendees. The instruction 'do not add information I didn't provide' helps but doesn't eliminate this risk — verify every specific claim (names, dates, commitments) against the source.

sections.question: After a meeting, you extract 8 action items and ask Copilot to create ADO work items for all 8. Three of the action items have no assigned owner and two have no deadline. What should Copilot do, and what should you do?
options: Copilot should assign the unowned items to whoever made the most recent comment in the meeting
Copilot should create all 8 tickets with the information available, flag the 3 unowned and 2 deadline-less items, and you should resolve those 5 gaps before the tickets are useful
Copilot should not create any tickets until all information is complete
Copilot should guess at owners based on each person's workload
sections.explanation: The right behavior is to create what can be created (the information that exists is useful) and explicitly flag what's missing (so you know what to chase). Creating tickets with [UNASSIGNED] and [NO DEADLINE] placeholders makes the gaps visible — far better than not creating the tickets or silently leaving them blank. Your job is then to resolve the 5 gaps: find the meeting organizer or message attendees to assign ownership and agree on deadlines. An action item with no owner is not an action item — it's a hope.

sections.content: **Lesson 6-25 complete.** Meetings are one of the biggest time drains in organizational life — and most of that time is in the surrounding tasks, not the conversation itself. Pre-meeting briefing, structured note-taking, action item extraction, follow-up drafting, and ticket creation can all be automated or accelerated with Copilot. The conversation itself is yours — everything else doesn't need to be. Lesson 6-26 covers gathering and synthesizing information from your team — the intelligence layer that makes all your decisions and reports accurate.
